tests.name: BKT.SpecialHodgeSubvariety.test1
tests.statement: A proper extra-Hodge-tensor condition is admitted.

tests.name: BKT.SpecialHodgeSubvariety.test2
tests.statement: The identity morphism of the generic datum is excluded from the exceptional family.

tests.name: BKT.SpecialHodgeSubvariety.test3
tests.statement: The entire countable union is not automatically asserted definable.

items.name: Closed analytic images of Hodge morphisms
items.statement: An arithmetic Hodge morphism associated to a Hodge subdatum has proper map onto its image, and its image is a closed complex analytic subvariety of the target Hodge manifold. Its source and target are taken at compatible arithmetic levels.
items.locator: Implicit in §5, p. 934 ('As W is also a complex analytic subvariety'); not stated or cited in the paper
proofSteps: Prove the arithmetic properness assertion at compatible levels using reduction theory.
Use the proper holomorphic image theorem to obtain a closed analytic image.
items.note: The precise properness and analytic image inputs have not been fully source-decomposed; they cannot be replaced by definability alone.

items.name: Definability of each special Hodge subvariety
items.statement: Any special subvariety Y of S_{Γ,G,M} is an R_an,exp-definable subset of S_{Γ,G,M} (with the definable structure of Theorem 1.1(1), for the erratum the one attached to the canonical maximal compact K_t). The same argument, via erratum Corollary 1.3, gives R_alg-definability.
items.locator: §5, p. 933, from 'Theorem 1.1(3)' (read 1.1(2), E15) and the remark that Hodge morphisms are morphisms of arithmetic quotients; corrected input: erratum Corollary 1.3
proofSteps: The canonical Hodge compact subgroups satisfy the corrected morphism hypotheses.
Project the graph of the semialgebraic-definable arithmetic morphism to its image.

items.name: Countable supply of exceptional Hodge subdata
items.statement: For a fixed rational polarized Hodge datum there are countably many rational tensor conditions and rational Hodge subdata that can cut out exceptional Mumford–Tate groups, including their rational translates and arithmetic connected components. Their special images cover the exceptional Hodge locus.
items.locator: §1.4, p. 921 ('easily seen to be a countable union'); §5, p. 934 ('(countable) union of special subvarieties'; 'HL(S,V) coïncides with the preimage Φ_S^{-1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M}))'); asserted without proof
proofSteps: Tensor constructions on a finite-dimensional rational vector space have countably many rational tensors.
Use stabilizers of finite tensor families to enumerate rational subgroups and then the Hodge-subdatum condition.
Separate the tensors already of Hodge type at the generic point from exceptional tensors.
items.note: The tensor-stabilizer/Hodge-subdatum correspondence and component enumeration are still prerequisite proof leaves.

items.name: Algebraicity of each special-locus pullback
items.statement: For a pure polarized integral variation over smooth complex quasi-projective S with period map Φ, the preimage of any special Hodge subvariety is a closed algebraic subvariety of S.
proofSteps: Closed analyticity follows from the holomorphic period map and the closed analytic target image.
Its graph and the definable special image give a definable preimage in the algebraic structure of S.
Apply definable analytic Chow.

items.name: Algebraicity of the exceptional Hodge locus
items.statement: Theorem 1.6. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Z-Hodge structures on a smooth complex quasi-projective variety S (setting of §1.3). The special subvarieties of S associated to V are algebraic, i.e., the Hodge locus HL(S,V), the set of s ∈ S at which V_s has exceptional Hodge tensors, is a countable union of closed irreducible algebraic subvarieties of S.
items.locator: Theorem 1.6, stated §1.4, p. 922; proved §5, pp. 933–934 (new proof of [CDK95])
proofSteps: Enumerate the proper special Hodge images corresponding to exceptional tensors.
Apply algebraicity separately to each pullback.
Take the finite irreducible decomposition of each algebraic pullback and their countable union; never invoke closure of definable sets under countable unions.

items.name: Finiteness of definable connected components
items.statement: Every definable subset of R^n in an o-minimal expansion of the real field has finitely many connected components, each definable. This extends to finite definable atlases.
items.locator: §5, p. 934 (parenthetical 'in particular has finitely many connected components'); erratum §1.6.1 (infinitely many components ⇒ not definable); standard [VDD98]
proofSteps: Use o-minimal cell decomposition from LD.6.
Finite atlas gluing preserves finiteness.

items.name: Existing planned normal-crossing compactification
items.statement: A smooth complex quasi-projective variety has a smooth projective compactification whose reduced boundary is a simple normal-crossing divisor.
items.locator: §4.1, JAMS p. 928 (the paper says 'normal crossing divisor'; Hironaka gives simple normal crossings)
proofSteps: Import the characteristic-zero compactification and resolution construction from its existing owner.

items.name: Proper holomorphic image theorem
items.statement: The image of a proper holomorphic map of complex analytic spaces is a closed complex analytic subset of the target.
items.locator: Implicit in §5, p. 934 (analyticity of the special subvariety Y, hence of W); Remmert's proper mapping theorem, not cited in the paper
proofSteps: Use the analytic-space/coherent-ideal foundations of ComplexComparisonPartII C0; the full Remmert proof remains a source-audit leaf.

items.name: Uniform arithmetic lattices have no nontrivial unipotents
items.statement: A cocompact lattice in the real points of a semisimple group contains no nonidentity unipotent element.
proofSteps: Import the precise lattice theorem; combined with quasi-unipotence it forces finite local monodromy.
items.note: Original Raghunathan proof not acquired in this checkpoint.

items.name: Restricted-analytic definability for a compact Hodge target
items.statement: If the arithmetic Hodge target of a pure polarized integral variation on smooth complex quasi-projective S is compact, then its period map is R_an-definable. At a torsion-free target level, finite local monodromy in the adjoint target is trivial; after the needed finite level cover the period map extends across a normal-crossing compactification.
proofSteps: Cocompactness and quasi-unipotence give finite monodromy at every boundary component.
At the appropriate finite cover use the extension theorem for trivial monodromy, retaining the distinction between the original variation and the adjoint target.
An analytic map on the compactification has an R_an-definable graph in finite buffered charts, and finite descent recovers the original map.
items.note: Finite global level-cover and extension details remain to be decomposed; no claim of a compact-target proof independent of the Hodge degeneration inputs.

items.name: Properness of the finite relation on Siegel closures
items.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff semialgebraic space with a group acting by semialgebraic homeomorphisms. Let C₁,…,C_r⊂X be closed semialgebraic subsets. Assume for each ordered pair only finitely many group elements have γC_i∩C_j≠∅. Then on C=⊔C_i the orbit relation E⊂C×C is semialgebraic, closed, and both coordinate projections E→C are proper.
items.locator: Published §3.1, p.926; expanded proof of the proper-relation assertion
proofSteps: For each pair i,j and its finite set of γ, the relation piece is the graph y=γx restricted to the closed domain C_i∩γ⁻¹C_j. It is closed and semialgebraic.
There are finitely many pairs and witnesses, so their union is closed and semialgebraic.

Over a compact subset K of the tagged C_i, each graph piece is homeomorphic to the closed subset K∩γ⁻¹C_j, hence compact. Finite union proves the first projection proper; inversion of γ proves the second.
Specialize C_i to the closures of the selected fixed-K Siegel sets. This proves properness only; a finite manifold atlas still needs a local-slice/refinement theorem.
items.note: Derived planning lemma, not asserted as a separately numbered result of the source.
acceptance: If one piece contains x and γx, they remain identified; injectivity of a whole piece is not assumed.
An open interval piece need not give a proper projection when its orbit meets an omitted endpoint: closedness is used.
Empty overlaps contribute no graph; the trivial group yields the diagonal relation.

items.name: Morphism of arithmetic quotients (original definition)
items.statement: Given arithmetic-quotient data (G′, G′ = G′(R)^+, M′, Γ′) and (G, G = G(R)^+, M, Γ) as in §1.1, a morphism of arithmetic quotients (φ, g): S_{Γ′,G′,M′} → S_{Γ,G,M} is the real analytic map Γ′h′M′ ↦ Γφ(h′)gM. Here φ: G′ → G is a morphism of semi-simple linear algebraic Q-groups and g ∈ G, with φ(Γ′) ⊂ Γ and φ(M′) ⊂ gMg^{-1}. These two conditions are exactly what makes the map well defined: φ(γ′h′m′)gM = γφ(h′)g(g^{-1}φ(m′)g)M.
items.note: Used in (1.1), where the middle Hecke map is the morphism (Int(g), g), in the false original Theorem 1.1(2) (E6), and in §5 ('any Hodge morphism ... is in particular a morphism of arithmetic quotients'). B's compatible-morphism is the erratum's restriction: it adds φ(K′) ⊂ gKg^{-1} and θ_{gKg^{-1}} stabilising φ(g′). It can take this as its base notion. Missing: routed to route 7.

items.name: Fundamental set for Γ acting on G/M
items.statement: A fundamental set for the action of Γ on G/M is a subset F ⊂ G/M such that Γ·F = G/M and the set {γ ∈ Γ : γF ∩ F ≠ ∅} is finite.
items.locator: Used without definition in Theorem 1.1(1), p. 919; the [PS13]/[KUY16] discussion, p. 919; Example 1.2, p. 920; §3.1, p. 926; also Theorem 1.1(1), p. 919; §3.1, p. 926 (𝓕 := ⋃𝔖_i); erratum Theorem 1.2(1) and Remark 1.1(3), pp. 2–3
items.note: Standard (Borel) meaning, supplied here. For F a finite union of Siegel sets the covering is Proposition 2.7(1) and the finiteness is Proposition 2.7(2) (B's siegel-finite-cover and siegel-finite-overlap). The 'in particular' clause of Theorem 1.1(1) stays true even if only Γ·F = G/M is intended. Planned: AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.3 plans Siegel sets and the covering of arithmetic quotients by finitely many of them.

items.name: R_an-definable sets are the globally subanalytic sets
items.statement: A subset of R^n is R_an-definable if and only if it is globally subanalytic, i.e. subanalytic in the compactification P^n(R) of R^n. In particular a relatively compact semi-analytic subset of R^n, and the graph of a real analytic map restricted to a relatively compact semi-analytic set whose closure lies in its domain, are R_an-definable.
items.note: A cited black box with no reference in the paper (van den Dries 1986; Denef–van den Dries 1988). Used in Example 1.2 ('not globally subanalytic'), in Lemma 4.2 (p. 929: 'Ψ is the restriction to a relatively compact set of a real analytic map') and in the proof of Proposition A.2 (p. 935: 'relatively compact and semi-analytic, hence R_an-definable'), which D's compact-corners-definable and buffered-transition-graph rely on. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Canonical R_alg-definable structure of a complex algebraic variety
items.statement: A smooth complex algebraic variety S carries a canonical R_alg-definable manifold structure coming from its complex algebraic structure. Cover S by finitely many affine open subvarieties U_i ⊂ C^{N_i} = R^{2N_i}. These are real algebraic sets with regular (hence semialgebraic) transition maps, and they can be refined to a finite atlas of semialgebraic charts onto open subsets of R^{2 dim S}. The result is independent of the choices up to definable equivalence. Regular maps between varieties, e.g. finite étale covers, are R_alg-definable. For S ⊇ R_alg (here R_an,exp) S gets the S-definable structure given by the same atlas.
items.locator: §1.3, p. 920 (before Theorem 1.3); Theorem 4.13, p. 933 ('hence endowing the C-analytic manifold S with a canonical R_alg-definable manifold structure')
items.note: Used without construction. It is the source structure in Theorem 1.3 (C's global-period-definability, 'relative to the algebraic definable structure on S') and the structure in which Theorem 4.13 is applied (D's definable-analytic-chow). No existing item covers it. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Arithmetic varieties are quasi-projective (Baily–Borel)
items.statement: Let G be of Hermitian type, so that X = G/K is a Hermitian symmetric domain, and let Γ ⊂ G(Q)^+ be a torsion-free arithmetic subgroup. Then S_{Γ,G,K} = Γ\G/K is the analytification of a smooth complex quasi-projective variety. It is Zariski open in its Baily–Borel compactification S̄^BB_{Γ,G,K}, which is a normal projective variety.
items.locator: §1.1, p. 917 ('this is a smooth complex quasi-projective variety'); §1.2, p. 919 ('its complex algebraic Baily–Borel compactification'); used in §4.6, p. 933; also §1.1, p. 917 (stated without citation); used in §4.6, p. 933 ('the smooth complex algebraic manifold S × S_{Γ,G,K}')
items.note: A cited black box, stated without reference (Baily–Borel 1966). Needed for Remarks 1.4(2) and Theorem 4.12 (D's borel-algebraicity), whose target must carry an algebraic structure, and for hermitian-structure-comparison. Planned: ShimuraVarieties V2 plans the Baily–Borel theorem and the algebraic structure of arithmetic quotients of Hermitian domains.

items.name: Generic Mumford–Tate group and Mumford–Tate domain of a variation
items.statement: For s ∈ S, the Mumford–Tate group MT(V_s) of the polarized Z-Hodge structure V_s is the smallest Q-algebraic subgroup of GL(V_{s,Q}) whose real points contain the image of the Deligne torus h_s. Equivalently, it is the subgroup fixing all Hodge tensors of V_s. It is connected and reductive. There is a countable union Σ ⊊ S of proper closed analytic subvarieties such that, after parallel transport over the universal cover of S, MT(V_s) is a constant group for s ∉ Σ and contains MT(V_s) for every s. This constant group is the generic Mumford–Tate group MT(V). Let G be its adjoint group and G = G(R)^+. G acts holomorphically and transitively on the Mumford–Tate domain D = G/M (the G-orbit of a Hodge structure), with compact isotropy M.
items.note: Named but not defined in the paper, which refers to [K17]. Conventions (h_s on S or on U(1)) give the same adjoint group. B's hodge-datum and hodge-manifold and C's general-period-domain use G and D but do not define MT(V). Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Exceptional Hodge tensors and the Hodge locus HL(S, V)
items.statement: A Hodge tensor of V_s is a rational class in some tensor space V_{s,Q}^{⊗a} ⊗ (V_{s,Q}^∨)^{⊗b} that is of Hodge type (p, p). It is exceptional if it is not fixed by the generic Mumford–Tate group MT(V), i.e. if it is not a Hodge tensor at a general point. The Hodge locus HL(S, V) ⊂ S is the set of s ∈ S at which V_s has an exceptional Hodge tensor, equivalently at which MT(V_s) ⊊ MT(V).
items.note: The object of Theorem 1.6 (D's hodge-locus-algebraicity). In §5 (p. 934) the paper identifies it with Φ_S^{-1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M})). No existing item defines it. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: The Hodge locus is a countable union of analytic subvarieties (special subvarieties of S)
items.statement: HL(S, V) is a countable union of irreducible closed complex analytic subvarieties of S. These are called the special subvarieties of S associated to V.
items.note: Asserted without proof. The standard argument: the locus where a given flat multivalued integral tensor is Hodge is closed analytic on each simply connected open set, and there are countably many integral tensors modulo monodromy. The paper's notion of 'special subvariety of S' is only this implicit one. Its §5 proof really treats the preimages Φ_S^{-1}(Y) of special subvarieties Y of S_{Γ,G,M}. Overlaps with D's rational-hodge-countability and could be merged there. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Compact linear groups are real algebraic
items.statement: Every compact subgroup M of the real points of a linear algebraic ℝ-group 𝐆_ℝ (in particular a compact subgroup of G = 𝐆(ℝ)⁺) is the group of real points of a real algebraic subgroup 𝐌_ℝ ⊂ 𝐆_ℝ (its Zariski closure): M = 𝐌_ℝ(ℝ). In particular M is a semi-algebraic subset of G.
items.locator: Remark 2.2, p. 922; [OV90, Th. 5, p. 133]; used in both proofs of Lemma 2.1, p. 923
items.note: Black box. The algebraic proof needs 𝐌_ℝ to apply Chevalley's theorem. The o-minimal proof needs M semi-algebraic for E = {(g,gm)} to be semi-algebraic, which the paper takes for granted. Missing: routed to route 7.

items.name: Comparison of Siegel-set conventions for a fixed K
items.statement: Fix a maximal compact K ⊂ 𝐆(ℝ). Every Siegel set U × A_{P,t} × W associated to a ℚ-parabolic 𝐏 and K (Definition 2.3) is contained in a Siegel set ΩA_{t′}K in Orr's sense for a Siegel triple (𝐏₀,𝐒₀,K) with 𝐏₀ ⊂ 𝐏 a minimal ℚ-parabolic. Conversely, every such Orr Siegel set is contained in a Siegel set for 𝐏₀ and K in the sense of Definition 2.3. Moreover every Siegel set for K is contained in a 𝐆(ℚ)-translate of a Siegel set for K and one fixed minimal ℚ-parabolic.
items.locator: Implicit in the erratum's proof of Theorem 1.2(2), p. 3 (applying [4, Theorem 1], stated for Orr's Siegel sets, [Orr18, §2.B]); cf. BGST 2021, §3.1–3.2
items.note: This bridge is stated in neither the paper nor the erratum. Proof: write m ∈ W as n′a′m′k′ in M_P with respect to 𝐏₀ ∩ 𝐋_P; A_P is central in L_P, so uam k = (un′)(aa′)m′(k′k), and the simple roots of 𝐏₀ are bounded below on aa′ because a′ lies in a compact set. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Factorisation of a morphism with a choice of maximal compact
items.statement: Every morphism (φ,g) : S_{Γ′,G′,M′,K′} → S_{Γ,G,M,K} with a choice of maximal compact factors as R_g ∘ ι ∘ σ. Here σ = (φ̄,1) : S_{Γ′,G′,M′,K′} → S_{φ(Γ′),H,φ(M′),φ(K′)} is induced by the surjection φ̄ : 𝐆′ → 𝐇 := φ(𝐆′); ι = (incl,1) : S_{φ(Γ′),H,φ(M′),φ(K′)} → S_{Γ,G,gMg⁻¹,gKg⁻¹} is induced by 𝐇 ⊂ 𝐆; and R_g = (id,g) : S_{Γ,G,gMg⁻¹,gKg⁻¹} → S_{Γ,G,M,K}, ΓhgMg⁻¹ ↦ ΓhgM. Each factor is again a morphism with a choice of maximal compact, and R_g is ℝ_alg-definable by erratum Remark 1.1(1).
items.locator: §3.2, p. 927 (printed reduction (f,g) = (Int(g⁻¹)∘f,1)∘(Int(g),g), see E18) and p. 928 (reduction to inclusions); erratum, proof of Theorem 1.2, p. 3 ('As in [2] we reduce to φ : 𝐆′ → 𝐆 injective')
items.note: Corrected form of the paper's reduction, which needs g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ) (E18). φ(Γ′) ⊂ Γ is torsion-free and arithmetic in 𝐇; φ(K′) is maximal compact in H; θ_{gKg⁻¹} stabilises 𝔥 = φ(𝔤′) by hypothesis. Missing: routed to route 7.

items.name: Siegel sets under a surjective morphism
items.statement: Let φ : 𝐆′ → 𝐇 be a surjective morphism of connected semisimple ℚ-groups, K′ ⊂ G′ maximal compact and K_H = φ(K′). For every ℚ-parabolic 𝐏′ of 𝐆′, φ(𝐏′) is a ℚ-parabolic of 𝐇, and φ maps each Siegel set of G′ associated to 𝐏′ and K′ into a Siegel set of H associated to φ(𝐏′) and K_H. Consequently (φ,1) : S_{Γ′,G′,M′,K′} → S_{φ(Γ′),H,φ(M′),K_H} is ℝ_alg-definable.
items.locator: §3.2, p. 928, surjective case (replacing the printed product decomposition, see E19)
items.note: Repair, not a statement of the paper. Up to isogeny 𝐆′ = 𝐇 × 𝐇₂ and 𝐏′ = 𝐏₁ × 𝐏₂. Then φ(A_{P′,t}) = A_{P₁,t}, φ(N_{P′}) = N_{P₁} and φ(W′) ⊂ M_{P₁}K_H is bounded. Definability follows from Theorem 1.2(1) for H. Missing: routed to route 7.

items.name: Finite semi-algebraic atlas from Siegel pieces
items.statement: Let Γ be torsion-free and let 𝔖₁,…,𝔖_k be semi-algebraic Siegel sets for the fixed K whose images cover S_{Γ,G,M}. There are finitely many open semi-algebraic sets O₁,…,O_m ⊂ G/M, each a Γ-translate of a subset of some slightly enlarged open Siegel set, such that π|_{O_j} is injective and open and the π(O_j) cover S_{Γ,G,M}. Composed with semi-algebraic charts of G/M (horospherical coordinates on the Siegel ends), the inverses (π|_{O_j})⁻¹ form a finite ℝ_alg-definable atlas whose structure is the one of §3.1.
items.locator: §3.1, p. 926 (claim that the V_i 'form an explicit finite open atlas', see E23)
items.note: Repair of E23, not in the paper. For t ≫ 0 only Γ_P = Γ ∩ P identifies points of 𝔖 (Proposition 2.7(4)). Γ_P has trivial A_P-component and acts freely and properly discontinuously on the (n,m)-coordinates, so small U′ × A_{P,t} × W′ pieces are injective. The remaining part of each 𝔖_i has bounded A-coordinate, is relatively compact and needs finitely many small balls. Missing: routed to route 7.

items.name: Uniformizing strip S_H and lifted period map
items.statement: Let H be the upper half-plane, e(z) = exp(2πiz): H → Δ* the universal cover of the punctured unit disk, and S_H = {x+iy ∈ H : 0 < x < 1, y > 1}, 'the usual Siegel fundamental set'. Put p = e(·)^n: H^n → (Δ*)^n. For Φ: (Δ*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}, Φ̃: H^n → D = G/M is the lift with π∘Φ̃ = Φ∘p. p|S_H^n is R_an,exp-definable, and p(S_H^n) = {0 < |q_j| < e^(−2π), q_j ∉ R_(>0)}.
items.note: Used in Lemma 4.2, Remark 4.3, Definition 4.4 (Σ_n ⊂ S_H^n) and §4.5. The open strip misses x = 0 (new sourceIssue); bounded-sector does not define S_H. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Hodge-form functions h(u,v) on Σ_n
items.statement: For u, v ∈ V_C let h(u,v): Σ_n → C be z ↦ h_z(u,v) := Q_C(C_z u, conj v), where C_z is the Weil operator of the Hodge structure Φ̃(z) on V_C (C_z = i^(p−q) on H^(p,q)). Put h_z(u) := h_z(u,u), which is > 0 for u ≠ 0. The printed text omits the conjugation (new sourceIssue).
items.note: This is the object of Proposition 4.6, Lemma 4.7 and Theorem 4.8. The existing hodge-form item is the library form, not this function of z. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Definability of π∘Φ̃ on S_H^n and of Φ on p(S_H^n)
items.statement: Suppose Φ̃(S_H^n) ⊂ ∪_(i∈I) 𝔖_i for finitely many Siegel sets 𝔖_i ⊂ G/M associated with the fixed canonical maximal compact K (Theorem 1.5 with erratum §1.5). Each π|𝔖_i: 𝔖_i → S_{Γ,G,M,K} is R_alg-definable (Theorem 1.1(1), erratum Theorem 1.2(1)), and Φ̃|S_H^n is R_an,exp-definable (Lemma 4.2). Hence π∘Φ̃|S_H^n is R_an,exp-definable. So Φ|p(S_H^n) is R_an,exp-definable, because its graph is the image of a definable graph under p × id.
items.locator: §4.2, JAMS p. 929, the paragraph after Remark 4.3
items.note: This is the step that finishes the proof of Theorem 4.1. The printed text cites Theorem 1.1(2) here (E12). Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Norm estimates are independent of the adapted splitting (Kashiwara)
items.statement: Let {W^1,…,W^n} be a distributive family of increasing filtrations of a finite-dimensional real (or complex) vector space M, and put W_α = ∩_j W^j_(α_j). Let f_α ≥ 0 be functions on a set T with f_β ≤ C f_α for β ≤ α, and let |·|_t (t ∈ T) be norms. Consider the condition that there is C > 0 with |u|_t ≤ C Σ_α f_α(t)|u_α| and Σ_α f_α(t)|u_α| ≤ C|u|_t for all u = Σ u_α (u_α ∈ I_α) and all t. This condition does not depend on the choice of splitting M = ⊕ I_α with W_α = ⊕_(β≤α) I_β. It is written |u|_t ∼ f_α(t) on u ∈ W_α.
items.note: Theorem 4.8 is stated for the rational splitting J but applied in Lemma 4.7 to the complex splitting I^α. This result is what justifies that (new sourceIssue). Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Definable extension of a continuous map from a dense definable subset
items.statement: Let X, Y be definable, Φ: X → Y continuous, and U ⊂ X a dense definable subset with Φ|U definable. Then Φ is definable, since graph(Φ) = closure(graph(Φ|U)) ∩ (X × Y).
items.locator: Used implicitly in §4.1 (the reduction to r_i = n, l_i = 0), JAMS p. 928, and needed to fill the rays arg q_j = 0 missed by p(S_H^n), p. 929
items.note: A one-line input for the repairs in the new §4.1 and §4.2 issues. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Definability descends through the coordinate-power cover
items.statement: Let c: (Δ*)^n → (Δ*)^n, c(q) = (q_1^(m_1), …, q_n^(m_n)). If Φ∘c is R_an,exp-definable, then so is Φ, because graph(Φ) = (c × id)(graph(Φ∘c)) and c is semialgebraic. c maps (Δ*_ρ)^n onto (Δ*_(ρ^m))^n.
items.locator: §4.2, JAMS p. 928 ('Replacing (Δ*)^n by a finite étale cover if necessary')
items.note: This step is implicit in the paper. local-period-definability mentions covers but no item states the descent. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Holomorphic maps to arithmetic varieties are period maps
items.statement: Let S be a smooth complex quasi-projective variety and f : S → S_{Γ,G,K} a holomorphic map to an arithmetic variety (G of Hermitian type, Γ neat arithmetic). Then, after replacing S by a finite étale cover, f = ι ∘ Φ_S. Here Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S, V) is the period map of the polarized Z-VHS V = f^*𝕍, where 𝕍 is the VHS on D = G/K defined by a faithful Q-representation of G with a Γ-stable lattice, horizontal because D is Hermitian symmetric. ι : Hod^0(S,V) → S_{Γ,G,K} is a Hodge morphism. In particular f is R_an,exp-definable (Theorem 1.3 and erratum Corollary 1.3).
items.locator: §4.6, proof of Theorem 4.12, p. 933: 'The map f is a period map, hence is R_an,exp-definable by Theorem 1.3.'
items.note: Asserted without proof; see the new gap on this sentence. The Hodge morphism ι is where Theorem 1.1(2) (erratum Corollary 1.3) enters, which partly explains the heading of §4.6. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Hodge locus of a connected Hodge variety
items.statement: HL(S_{Γ,G,M}) is the (countable) union of the special subvarieties of S_{Γ,G,M}. Read: of the strict special subvarieties Y ≠ S_{Γ,G,M}; see E28.
items.note: The printed wording includes the image of the identity Hodge morphism (E28). Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: The Hodge locus of S is the preimage of the Hodge locus of the Hodge variety
items.statement: Let V be a pure polarized Z-VHS on smooth quasi-projective S with period map Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S,V) = S_{Γ,G,M} (after the finite étale cover of §1.3). Then HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M})) = ⋃_{Y strict special} Φ_S^{-1}(Y). Hence Theorem 1.6 reduces to the algebraicity of each Φ_S^{-1}(Y).
items.locator: §5, p. 934 ('The Hodge locus HL(S, V) coïncides with the preimage Φ_S^{-1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M})). Hence to prove Theorem 1.6 we are reduced to ...')
items.note: Asserted without proof (standard, [K17]). Overlaps the extraction's rational-hodge-countability ('their special images cover the exceptional Hodge locus'), which could absorb it instead. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Hodge-form map to the space of positive definite forms
items.statement: Let X be the space of positive definite symmetric bilinear forms on V_R. Let G′ ⊂ SL(V_Q) be a semisimple Q-group acting on V whose real points act transitively on D; the paper writes 'the natural embedding G(Q) ⊂ SL(V_Q)', and G′ = MT(V)^der works. Define ι: D → X by ι(x) = h_x, where h_x(u,v) = Q(C_x u, v) for u,v ∈ V_R and C_x is the Weil operator of x. ι is G′(R)^+-equivariant, factors through G′(R)^+/K with K = Stab(h_{x0}) ⊃ M, and takes values in the forms of Gram determinant |det Q|.
items.note: The central construction of §4.5. faithful-hodge-representation covers only the choice of group. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Set of (e,C)-reduced forms
items.statement: For an integral ordered basis e of V_Z and C > 0, T_{e,C} := {b ∈ X | b is (e,C)-reduced}.
items.note: Named in the paper; could be merged into reduced-form or reduction-siegel-dictionary. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Preimages of Siegel sets of X under ι
items.statement: For every Siegel set 𝔖 ⊂ X, ι^{-1}(𝔖) is contained in the union of finitely many Siegel sets of D, associated to the canonical maximal compact K = Stab(h_{x0}).
items.locator: §4.5, p. 932 (printed citation [B-HC62, 7.5]; erratum §1.5 replaces it by [BGST, Prop. 28.1])
items.note: Derivation: ι^{-1}(𝔖_{SL}·h_{x0}) = (𝔖_{SL}K_{SL} ∩ G′(R)^+)·x0. Apply BGST 28.1 (item rational-siegel-pullback) with H = G′ ⊂ SL(V). Its forward-containment hypothesis is Orr–Schnell Thm 1, which applies because K = G′(R) ∩ SO(h_{x0}) and θ_{h_{x0}} = Ad(C_{x0}) stabilizes 𝔤′. Siegel sets for G′ and for the adjoint G give the same subsets of D (central isogeny). Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Images of Siegel sets of D under ι
items.statement: Every Siegel set of D (and of the full period domain of (V,Q)) is mapped by ι into the union of finitely many Siegel sets of X.
items.locator: §4.5, proof of the Claim, p. 933 ('by Theorem 3.2')
items.note: Apply Theorem 3.2 to G′ ⊂ SL(V), or to Aut(V,Q) ⊂ SL(V) when the n = 1 input is Schmid's result for the full period domain. c·𝔖 for c ∈ SL(V_Q) is a Siegel set of X. The erratum's dependence on K does not arise here: Theorem 3.2 as printed only asserts that some Siegel set of the big group exists, and Siegel sets of X do not depend on K. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Griffiths transversality for the lift γ = e^{z·N}e^{v(t)}
items.statement: With Φ̃(z) = γ(z)F, γ(z) = e^{z·N}e^{v(t)}, t = p(z), horizontality of Φ̃ is equivalent to γ^{-1}∂γ/∂z_i ∈ F^{-1}𝔤 for all i. Since ∂t_i/∂z_i = 2πi t_i, this reads e^{-ad v(t)}N_i + 2πi t_i ((1−e^{-ad v(t)})/ad v(t)) ∂v/∂t_i ∈ F^{-1}𝔤.
items.locator: Lemma 4.10 proof, p. 932 (printed without the factor 2πi)
items.note: Input to horizontal-perturbation. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Monodromy logarithms are (−1,−1)-morphisms of the limiting MHS
items.statement: For the Deligne splitting 𝔤^{p,q} of the mixed Hodge structure on 𝔤 induced by (F, W(M_n)), each N_i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) lies in 𝔤^{-1,-1}.
items.note: Black box from [CKS86]. Each N_i satisfies N_iF^p ⊂ F^{p-1}, and N_iW(M_n)_k ⊂ W(M_n)_{k-2} because N_i lies in the closure of the cone whose interior contains M_n. So N_i is a real morphism of MHS of type (−1,−1), and functoriality of the Deligne splitting gives N_i ∈ 𝔤^{-1,-1}. Missing: routed to route 8.

items.name: Endomorphisms commuting with N preserve W(N)
items.statement: If N is nilpotent on a finite-dimensional vector space and A commutes with N, then A W(N)_k ⊂ W(N)_k for all k. In particular an endomorphism commuting with N_1,…,N_j preserves W(M_j).
items.locator: Lemma 4.10 proof, p. 932 ('Thus, v_i(t) preserves each W(M_j) for j < i'; likewise for g_i)
items.note: Used without comment. Proof: complete N to an sl_2-triple. ker(ad N) on End(V) consists of lowest-weight vectors, which have ad H-weight ≤ 0. Missing: routed to route 8.

routes.title: Arithmetic locally symmetric spaces and their cohomology, Part II: tame arithmetic quotients
routes.reason: ALS.2 owns the symmetric M=K Borel–Serre compactification. General compact stabilizers M⊂K, fixed-K definable structures and their corrected functoriality require an extension of those objects, not a second reduction-theory roadmap.
routes.brief: Import Arithmetic locally symmetric spaces and their cohomology (ArithmeticLocallySymmetricSpaces ALS.0 and ALS.2), Adelic algebraic groups and arithmetic quotients (AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.3), Logic, definability, valued fields and motivic integration (LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory LD.0/LD.6), and the upstream Lie groups roadmap (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/LieGroups Layer 9). For connected semisimple rational G, torsion-free arithmetic Γ, connected compact M and a chosen maximal compact K containing M, construct the R_alg-definable structure on Γ\G/M characterized by fixed-K Siegel charts. For neat Γ construct the general Borel–Serre analytic manifold with corners and prove that its compactification induces the same R_an structure on the interior. Specializing M=K must recover ALS.2. Prove semialgebraic definability of the corrected morphisms (φ,g), with rational φ, the level/stabilizer/compact inclusions and target Cartan involution preserving the image Lie algebra. Use corrected Orr–Schnell containment and BGST Proposition28.1 with its forward-containment hypothesis. Prove Hecke definability and the canonical symmetric-space formulation. Decompose the semialgebraic homogeneous quotient, finite proper equivalence relation, local slice refinement, boundary gluing and nonsurjective/surjective morphism adapters. Never assert K-independence for a fixed general Γ\G/M or functoriality of Borel–Serre compactifications. Tests must include SL₂ with two compact choices, the Cartan-unstable torus, rank-zero boundary and the M=K specialization. Suggested later file: TauCeti/NumberTheory/ArithmeticQuotient/Definability.lean. This is a partial design brief with the explicit source gaps below. Corrections the design must carry: the first proof of Lemma 2.1 fails unless M is normal, so the semialgebraic model of G/M must come from the proper-quotient proof or an orbit G(ℝ)·v (E8); Definition 2.5, Proposition 2.7 and Theorem 1.1 hold only with Siegel sets for one fixed maximal compact K, and only morphisms compatible with the chosen compacts are definable, as the 2023 erratum corrects (E5, E6); §3.2's reduction to g = e and its surjective case need the compact-data transport and a compact-stabilizer quotient adapter (E18, E19); §3.1's Siegel pieces are not injective charts until refined (E23); and Remark 3.1 is false: in the paper's own corner coordinates the Borel–Serre compactification is ℝ_alg-definable (E42).

routes.title: Hodge structures (pure, mixed, and polarized), Part II: degeneration, period maps and Hodge loci
routes.reason: Upstream HodgeStructures L0–L3 supplies pure/mixed structures, polarizations, Deligne splitting and period-domain points, all largely built. It explicitly reserves the period-domain manifold structure for a successor. The multivariable degeneration, non-Hermitian domain geometry and period-map/locus theorems therefore extend this direction.
routes.brief: Import Hodge structures (pure, mixed, and polarized) (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/HodgeStructures L0–L3) through the pinned carriers, positive Hodge form, Weil operator and Deligne decomposition; import the general polarized-variation definition from ShimuraData D3, normal-crossing compactifications from AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry R09.7d, rational reduction from AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.3, analytic spaces from ComplexComparisonPartII C0, and definable geometry/Chow from LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory LD.6. Use ArithmeticQuotientDefinability for corrected fixed-K quotient structures. Construct the complex manifold and compact dual on the existing period-point carrier, the canonical Hodge Cartan involution and compatible Hodge morphisms. Prove Theorem1.5: for a local unipotent pure polarized integral variation and any bounded real width R and positive height η, the lifted period map on H_(R,η)^n lies in finitely many fixed-canonical-K Siegel sets. Establish nilpotent extension, centered monodromy weights, simultaneous rational and complex splittings, both Kashiwara norm estimates, the horizontal correction, indefinite Gram determinant formulas, rough entries and finite-permutation reducedness. Establish the faithful adjoint/central-cover representation adapter before using SL(V) reduction. Then prove Theorem1.3: every such variation on smooth complex quasi-projective S has an R_an,exp-definable period map. Local use must shrink and buffer disks and cover angular seams. Finally prove Theorem1.6: the exceptional Hodge locus is a countable union of closed irreducible algebraic subvarieties, through closed analytic proper special images and definable Chow applied individually to their pullbacks. Exclude the generic identity subdatum; do not call the countable union definable. Supply Borel algebraicity only as an imported/alternative proof at ShimuraVarieties V3. Tests include zero monodromy, the zero-vector exclusion, weight shifts, conjugation conventions, a non-Hermitian domain, reversed reduced bases and the outer-boundary period-map example. Suggested later file: TauCeti/Geometry/Hodge/Variation/DefinablePeriodMap.lean. The repaired widened-sector curve lemma and quantitative finite-permutation basis transfer are supplied. Original analytic inputs, their bounded-real-width uniformity, and finite boundary-chart adapters remain open in this partial brief. Corrections the design must carry: Theorem 4.1 is false on the whole unit polydisk and holds after shrinking, the proof failing at the reduction on p. 929 (E1); roughly polynomial functions form a ring only when denominators are roughly monomial polynomials (E46); Theorem 4.8 must be stated in Kashiwara's splitting-independent, multigraded form, since Lemmas 4.7 and 4.10 apply it to vectors of the complex splitting (E49, E54); Lemma 4.10's lower bound is proved only for large y_n, so it and its consequences hold on a shrunken polydisk (E53); §4.5 proves Theorem 1.5 only on 𝔖^n_𝔥 after shrinking (E56); the Claim on p. 933 is false for every basis and must be replaced by conditions (1) and (3) for one basis, giving finitely many orderings (E3, E60); the rational Siegel pullback is BGST Proposition 3.4, not [B-HC62, 7.5] (E7); and in §4.6 the proof of Theorem 4.12 must show that f is a period map (E58) and that the Theorem 1.1 structure and the Baily–Borel structure on S_{Γ,G,K} agree after expansion to ℝ_an,exp (E59), and restrict to smooth S or add a descent (E29).

sourceIssues.locator: Theorem 4.1, JAMS p. 928; the failing step is on p. 929 ('We are reduced to proving that the composition …'); author pp. 13–14
sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (Δ*)^n, with period map Φ : (Δ*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable.
sourceIssues.correction: Restrict to smaller polydisks: for every 0 < ρ < 1, Φ restricted to (Δ*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable. The printed proof gives ρ = e^(−2π), once 0 < x < 1 is replaced by 0 ≤ x < 1 (see E45). For general ρ < 1: cover the closed ρ-polydisk, which is compact in Δ^n, by finitely many small polydisk charts centred at its points, each of the form (Δ*)^r × Δ^l, and apply the local statement in each chart. Alternatively, rerun §4.2 on {0 ≤ x < 1, y > η} with η = −(log ρ)/2π. That uses Theorem 1.5 for this η, and its printed proof (§4.5, on Σ_n with y > 1) needs the same compactness step. §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover S̄.
sourceIssues.reason: The counterexample holds; I rechecked it by hand and numerically. With f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)), τ = 2i + εf and trivial monodromy, the fibre over π(2i + ε/e) is {z_n = 2πin/(2+2πin) : n ≠ 0}, an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1. The fibre of a definable map would have finitely many components. Δ is the unit disk (p. 922), and e(·) maps H onto the unit Δ* (p. 929). Where the proof fails: Lemma 4.2 is true as stated with no shrinking, because Schmid (4.12) (p. 233) says Ψ extends holomorphically to the whole open Δ^n, and p(S_H^n) lies in the compact polydisk |q_j| ≤ e^(−2π). The failing step is the reduction 'We are reduced to proving that the composition S_H^n → G/M → S_{Γ,G,M} is R_an,exp-definable'. That reduction controls Φ only on p(S_H^n) ⊂ (Δ*_(e^(−2π)))^n. The earlier correction's 'then for every ρ<1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces' is inaccurate for n ≥ 2: {ρ ≤ |q_1| < ρ'} × (Δ*)^(n−1) is not compact. The author copy is identical. The erratum does not mention this; §1.5 calls the proof of Theorem 1.3 correct apart from the §4.5 citation. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected.

review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotation matches p. 928 (author copy p. 13 identical). Δ is the unit disk (p. 922) and e(·) is the uniformization of the unit Δ* (p. 929), so the theorem concerns the whole unit punctured polydisk. Counterexample rechecked: (1+z)/(1−z) maps Δ onto Re w > 0, so f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) has |f| < 1. τ = 2i + εf is the period map of a weight-one Z-PVHS on Δ, with trivial monodromy on Δ*. For torsion-free Γ, π is injective on B(2i, ε) when ε is small, so Φ^(−1)(π(2i+ε/e)) = {z ∈ Δ* : f(z) = 1/e} = {z_n = 2πin/(2+2πin) : n ≠ 0}. Here f(z_n) = e^(−1−2πin) = e^(−1) exactly, |z_n| < 1 and z_n → 1 (also checked numerically). An infinite discrete fibre is not definable, so Theorem 4.1 is false as printed. The revised diagnosis is right. Schmid (4.12) (p. 233, checked in the local copy) says Ψ extends holomorphically to all of Δ^k. p(𝔖_H^n) ⊂ {|q_j| < e^(−2π)} is relatively compact in Δ^n, so Lemma 4.2 holds with no shrinking. The failing step is the reduction to 𝔖_H^n, which controls Φ only on p(𝔖_H^n). The criticism of the old correction is also right: for n ≥ 2, {ρ ≤ |q_1| < ρ'} × (Δ*)^(n−1) is not compact, so compactness has to be applied to the closed polydisk inside Δ^n, using local charts. Of the two routes in the revised correction, the covering route is self-contained. The η-route relies on Theorem 1.5 for small η. Theorem 1.5 is stated for every η > 0 (p. 921), but §4.5 proves it only on Σ_n (y > 1), so the η-route needs the same compactness step. The erratum is silent. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected once the charts are buffered. The kind 'error' and reach 'a stated result' are right.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 4.5 proof, JAMS p.930; author p.15
sourceIssues.printed: "Consider for each positive integer m and real number c the function f_{m,c} which we obtain from f by setting z_1 = mz_2 + c. Note that the assumptions of the lemma still apply to f_{m,c}, and it follows by induction on n that f_{m,c} ≪ 1 on all of Σ_{n−1}"
sourceIssues.correction: State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on wider sectors Σ_n^R={|x_i|<R,y₁≥⋯≥y_n>1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution maps Σ_(n−1)^R′ into Σ_n^(mR′+|c|). The application needs original-source bounded-real-width uniformity for Schmid Corollary 5.29 and the CKS/Kashiwara norm estimates; G3 records that this is still unverified. The R-quantifier of the target Theorem 1.5 is not evidence for its prerequisites.
sourceIssues.reason: Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation.

review.reason: Checked on the page images and independently. Proposition 2.7(2) as printed, with the basepoints free, is false. Take 𝐆 = SL₂, Γ = SL₂(ℤ), 𝐏₁ = 𝐏₂ the upper triangular subgroup, 𝔖₁ = U₁A_{t₁}K_{iv} (v ≠ 1; the diagonal torus is θ_{iv}-stable) and 𝔖₂ = U₂A_{t₂}SO₂ with U₂ = {(1,b;0,1) : |b| < 1}. Then 𝔖₁·i ∋ s²z₀ for all s² > t₁, where z₀ = u₀+iy₀ ∈ K_{iv}·i has u₀ ≠ 0. So 𝔖₁ meets γ_n𝔖₂ for γ_n = (1,n;0,1) and all large n, and Γ_{𝔖₂,𝔖₁} is infinite. The step of §3.1 quoted above fails in the same way: γ𝔖 is associated to γx, and a Siegel set for another maximal compact is not contained in a Siegel set for K (erratum §1.6.1). With K fixed the step holds by Lemma 2.4 and erratum Remark 1.1(1). Author copy and arXiv v2 have the same text.

review.reason: Theorem 3.2 (= [O17, Thm 1.2] = Orr 2018 Thm 1.2) is correct as stated. It is existential in K_G, and Orr–Schnell (ANT 17 (2023) 1231) confirm the statement and supply the existence of K_G through Mostow. Known: erratum §1.5 replaces [B-HC62, 7.5] with [1, 28.1] 'as the former is for real Siegel sets'. I checked the replacement in BGST, arXiv:2112.06995v1. Prop. 28.1 there is Prop. 3.4 of the published version (Épijournal Géom. Algébrique 2023, Art. 1). Setting: H ⊆ G reductive over ℚ, with K_H = K_G ∩ H(ℝ). Hypothesis: every K_H-Siegel set of H lies in finitely many G(ℚ)-translates of a K_G-Siegel set of G. Conclusion: S_G ∩ H(ℝ) ⊆ F·S_H for some finite F ⊂ H(ℚ). BGST §28 itself says the result is 'similar to [BHC62, Lem. 7.5], except that we are working with Siegel sets for Q-algebraic groups (instead of with Siegel domains for R-algebraic groups)'. So the printed citation does not give the rational statement. The asserted inclusion is nevertheless true, so the step is unjustified rather than false, which makes it a gap; the revision to 'gap' is right. Hypothesis check: take H = G′ = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V) and K_G = SO(h_{x0}). For X ∈ 𝔤′, invariance of Q gives h(Xu,v) = −h(u, C X C^{−1} v). So θ_{K_G}(X) = −X^* = Ad(C_{x0})X, which lies in 𝔤′ because C_{x0} ∈ MT(ℝ). Also K_H = G′(ℝ) ∩ K_G. Orr–Schnell Thm 1 (the criterion quoted in erratum §1.3) then supplies the hypothesis. It follows that ι^{−1}(S_X) is the image of S̃_X ∩ G′(ℝ) ⊆ F·S_{G′}. That is finitely many G′(ℚ)-translates of a Siegel set of D, and each translate is again a Siegel set (Remark 2.6(1); for K-Siegel sets write g = k₀p₀ with p₀ ∈ P(ℝ)). The erratum's correction is right, but it applies only once a group acting on V is used (E27/E27).

sourceIssues.correction: Take each U_x to be a relatively compact semianalytic subset, open in R^n_k (e.g. a corner box), whose closure is compact inside the domain of a larger analytic chart φ'_x. Then {(u,v) ∈ cl U_x × cl U_y : φ'_x(u) = φ'_y(v)} is compact, and near each of its points it is the graph of an analytic extension of the transition. So the graph of the transition over U_x × U_y is bounded and semianalytic at every point of R^{2n}, hence globally subanalytic, i.e. R_an-definable. The same buffered argument proves the independence of choices (mixed transitions between two buffered atlases) and the R_an-definability of i_X (its local expressions in buffered charts of ∂X and X).

I re-derived the counterexample. F(x) = x + (x²/4)sin(1/x) on (0,1) has F'(x) = 1 + (x/2)sin(1/x) − (1/4)cos(1/x) ≥ 1/4, so F is an analytic diffeomorphism onto the bounded interval (0, 1 + sin(1)/4). F(x) = x exactly at x = 1/(nπ), n ≥ 1, an infinite discrete set, so F is not definable in any o-minimal structure. Take φ(t) = e^{iπt} on (0,1) and ψ = φ∘F^{-1}. Both are real analytic charts of S¹ with bounded semialgebraic domains. They are real analytically compatible in the paper's sense (p. 934: the transition ψ^{-1}∘φ = F extends analytically to an open neighbourhood of its domain), but they are not R_an-compatible. So the printed hypotheses (U_x relatively compact in R^n_k and semianalytic) do not give the 'immediate' implication. For the defence: a WLOG shrinking naturally stays inside the original chart domain, and with that buffer the implication holds (see the correction). So Proposition A.2 is true and the proof is repairable. But the buffer is neither stated nor implied by 'relatively compact in R^n_k': in the example above no shrinking is triggered. An adjoint group need not act on V. For a non-isotrivial family of elliptic curves, MT = GL_2 and G = PGL_2, and V = Q^2 is not a PGL_2-representation because −I ∈ SL_2 acts nontrivially. So §4 silently uses a different group. The revised fix works. A unipotent T_i lies in the identity component of the algebraic monodromy group, since the Zariski closure of the group a unipotent element generates is connected. That identity component lies in MT^der (Deligne/André). If one wants T_i ∈ MT(Q) first: the tensors defining the generic MT group become flat after a finite étale cover, and then the torus argument of the revision applies. MT^der ⊂ SL(V) is semisimple. A torsion-free Γ' ⊂ MT^der(Q) meets the finite centre trivially, so it maps isomorphically onto an arithmetic subgroup of G(Q). D and the rational parabolics and Siegel sets correspond under the central isogeny. The identification S_(Γ',G',M') ≅ S_(Γ,G,M) is a surjective morphism of arithmetic quotients, handled as in §3.2 (compatible with the Hodge-theoretic maximal compacts of erratum §1.4), so it is definable. Erratum §1.4 does take G to be the Q-Zariski closure of t(S¹) in GL(V_Q). The adapter is routine, uses only results in the paper and changes no statement. So the downgrade to 'nothing' is acceptable and consistent with the other routine gaps of this range. The kind 'gap' stands. The same place also has: The quotation matches the p. 932 image, and arXiv v2 reads the same. On p. 920, G is 'its associated adjoint semi-simple ℚ-group', the adjoint group of MT(V). An adjoint group need not act on V at all. Example: PGL_2 ≅ SO(3) has only odd-dimensional irreducible representations, so it has no faithful 2-dimensional representation and does not act on the standard weight-one V. There is therefore no 'natural embedding G(ℚ) ⊂ SL(V_ℚ)'. The map ι(x) = h_x itself is well defined without a group, but the comparison of Siegel sets through BGST 28.1 (E-E7) needs a subgroup of SL(V). The repair is routine. G′ = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V) is semisimple, and G′(ℝ)^+ → G(ℝ)^+ is surjective, so G′(ℝ)^+ acts transitively on D. ℚ-parabolics correspond under the central isogeny, N_P and A_P^0 map isomorphically, and the kernel is finite, so the Siegel sets of D defined by G′ and by G agree. The erratum's §1.4 reformulation uses G = ℚ-Zariski closure of t(S^1) ⊂ GL(V), consistent with this fix, but it does not amend §4.5. This is the same issue as E27 (T_i ∈ G(ℤ) ⊂ GL(V_ℤ), p. 928) at a further locator.

review.reason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: I checked the text on the images of pp. 933–934. By the definition on p. 933 the identity is a Hodge morphism, so S_{Γ,G,M} is itself special. Read literally, HL(S_{Γ,G,M}) = S_{Γ,G,M}, and the next sentence then gives HL(S,V) = S. That contradicts §1.4 (p. 921), where HL(S,V) is the set of points with exceptional Hodge tensors. The intended object is the union of the strict special subvarieties. Hod^0(S,V) is built from the generic Mumford–Tate group (§1.3), so Φ_S(S) is Hodge generic and HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(⋃_{Y strict} Y). The proof then shows that Φ_S^{-1}(Y) is algebraic for every special Y, strict or not, so nothing downstream changes. I endorse the revision from error to misprint: the qualifier is missing but the meaning is clear. One correction to the proposed reason: [K17] is not a source of the 'strict' convention. arXiv:1711.09387v1, the version cited, Definition 3.13 reads 'The Hodge locus HL(Y) of the connected mixed Hodge variety Y is the union of all special subvarieties of Y'. Its Proposition 3.20 states HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(Φ_S(S) ∩ HL(Hod^0(S,V))). So the paper inherits the same slip from [K17], while K17's own HL(S,V) (§§1.1, 2.6: the non-Hodge-generic points) matches the strict reading. The author copy has the same text, and the erratum is silent.

review.reason: Checked on the p. 918 image. The quote is exact, and the author copy is the same. The claim holds up under the paper's own definitions. The p. 917 definition of a morphism (φ, g) requires g ∈ G = G(R)^+. For (Int(g), g), the formula Γ'h'M ↦ Γ g h' g^{-1} g M = Γ g h' M is left multiplication by g. It satisfies φ(g^{-1}Γg ∩ Γ) = Γ ∩ gΓg^{-1} and φ(M) = gMg^{-1}, and it lands in G/M only if g ∈ G. For g ∈ G(Q) outside G(R)^+, which can happen when G(R) is disconnected (e.g. PGL_2, SO(p,q), and adjoint groups in general), left multiplication moves G(R)^+ to another component. So (Int(g), g) is then not a morphism. Theorem 1.1(2) on p. 919 correctly writes 'c_g, g ∈ G(Q)^+'. The commensuration part holds for all g ∈ G(Q), and the diagram (1.1) is correct for g ∈ G(Q)^+. Nuance: for some M a correspondence still exists for g ∉ G(Q)^+, e.g. (Int(g), 1) when M = {1}, or (Int(g), g·k) with k in the maximal compact of G(R) when M = K. It is just not 'left multiplication by g, i.e. (Int(g), g)'. Hence the fix is G(Q)^+, not a failure of the Hecke-correspondence idea.

A torsion-free, infinitely generated Fuchsian group Γ gives a complete hyperbolic surface Γ\H with infinitely generated π_1. Such a surface is not homotopy equivalent to a finite CW complex, so it is not the interior of a compact manifold with boundary. The surrounding paragraph is about arithmetic quotients, so the omitted qualifier 'arithmetic' is clear from context. The text is motivational and never used. So this is a misprint, not an error: a dropped qualifier that makes a cited theorem read as false. The 'Hence ... non-singular semi-algebraic set' sentence inherits the same qualifier. Akbulut–King even gives a non-singular real algebraic set.

review.reason: All five quotes match the images (pp. 924, 925, 927), and the author copy and arXiv read the same. The paper defines 𝐆(ℚ)⁺ := 𝐆(ℚ) ∩ G (p. 917) and requires g ∈ G for a morphism (φ,g) (p. 917). Left multiplication by g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ) \ 𝐆(ℝ)⁺ maps G to the other coset gG, and G/M to gG/M. Such components exist, e.g. for 𝐆 = PGL₂, where diag(−1,1) ∈ 𝐆(ℚ). So Remark 2.6(1) ('g𝔖 is a Siegel set of G/M'), 'the left 𝐆(ℚ)-multiplication on G' (p. 925, against 'the left 𝐆(ℚ)⁺-action' earlier on the same page) and the morphism (Int(g),g) with Int(g)(h)g = gh (p. 927) all need g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ)⁺. For g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ)⁺ they hold: g·π(S) = π(gSg⁻¹), which is a Siegel set for (g𝐏g⁻¹, gx) with K_{gx} ⊃ (gh)M(gh)⁻¹. Lemma 2.4 leaves g unquantified. It holds for every g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ), since conjugation preserves G = 𝐆(ℝ)⁺ (a normal subgroup) and g𝐏g⁻¹ is rational. For a general real g it fails (g𝐏g⁻¹ need not be rational). Definition 2.5 is a slip only if one reads the identification G/gMg⁻¹ ≃ G/M as right translation (hgMg⁻¹ ↦ hgM, the reading that makes 'some g' meaningful). The identification induced by conjugation needs no restriction. The erratum rewrites Definition 2.5 with a fixed K ⊃ M and no g, so that part is superseded. The meaning is clear throughout, so kind misprint and affects nothing are right.

sourceIssues.printed: Although the \bar{𝔖_i}, 1 ≤ i ≤ k, are semi-algebraic, it is not true in general that S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M} admits a natural structure of ℝ_alg-definable manifolds with corners: if 𝐏 ⊂ 𝐐 are two parabolics of 𝐆 it follows from the proof of [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2] that the inclusion of the corner G(Q) ⊂ G(P) is real analytic but not semi-algebraic in general.
sourceIssues.correction: Delete the remark. In the corner coordinates of Proposition 2.8 the inclusion G(Q) ⊂ G(P) is (n_Q, u, y) ↦ (n_Qn′(y), (u·a′(y)^{-α}) on Δ_P^Q and a′(y)^{-α} on Δ_{P′}, m′(y)), which is semi-algebraic. The Γ-action is semi-algebraic as well, so S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M,K} carries an ℝ_alg-definable manifold-with-corners structure (for fixed K), compatible with Theorem 1.1(1).
sourceIssues.reason: The paper's own charts are the corner coordinates (n, e_P(a), m) (Proposition 2.8 and p. 925; §3.1 uses U × \bar{A_{P,t}} × W as analytic charts). On the dense open subset G of G(Q) the transition to P-coordinates is: invert the Q-horospherical map, then take P-horospherical coordinates. Both horospherical maps are semi-algebraic bijections given by multiplication, and e_P, e_Q are algebraic characters. Explicitly, if m_Q = n′a′m′ in the P ∩ L_Q decomposition of M_QK, then (n_Q,a_Q,m_Q) ↦ (n_Qn′, a_Qa′, m′). A continuous extension of a semi-algebraic map from a dense subset has as graph the closure of that graph cut to domain × target, so it is semi-algebraic. The Γ- and M-actions are semi-algebraic in these coordinates as well. Defence: I could not consult [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2]; if it uses other corner coordinates the remark may concern those, but then the p. 925 description would be inaccurate instead.

review.reason: The quote matches the p. 927 image, and the author copy and arXiv have the same remark ('real-analytic'). The remark is false for the structure the paper itself describes. On p. 925 (citing [BJ06a, Prop. 6.3]) the analytic structure of Ḡ^BS is given by the corner coordinates N_P × Ā_P × M_PK, with Ā_P = [0,∞)^r through e_P(a) = (a^{-α})_{α∈Δ_P} (2.4). §3.1 uses the charts U × \bar{A_{P,t}} × W. Take P ⊂ Q and let P′ be the parabolic of M_Q determined by P. Then N_P = N_QN_{P′}, A_P = A_Q × A_{P′} and M_P = M_{P′}. Also M_QK = N_{P′}A_{P′}(M_PK) uniquely, and the multiplication map N_{P′} × A_{P′} × M_PK → M_QK is a semi-algebraic bijection. So its inverse y ↦ (n′(y), a′(y), m′(y)) is semi-algebraic. Since A_Q is central in L_Q, g = n_Qa_Qy = (n_Qn′)(a_Qa′)m′. The simple roots split as Δ_P = Δ_{P′} ⊔ Δ_P^Q, where the roots in Δ_{P′} are trivial on A_Q and restriction to A_Q maps Δ_P^Q bijectively onto Δ_Q. The corner inclusion G(Q) ⊂ G(P) is therefore (n_Q, u, y) ↦ (n_Qn′(y), (u_{α|A_Q}·a′(y)^{-α})_{α∈Δ_P^Q} ∪ (a′(y)^{-α})_{α∈Δ_{P′}}, m′(y)). This formula is polynomial in u = e_Q(a_Q) and semi-algebraic in y, and it extends to u ∈ [0,∞)^{r_Q}. So the map is semi-algebraic (indeed Nash). For example, in SL₃ the A-components are square roots of sums of squares of minors of g. The Γ-action (more generally the 𝐆(ℚ)-action) in corner coordinates is semi-algebraic on the dense interior, being a composite of multiplications and inverse horospherical maps. A continuous map whose restriction to a dense semi-algebraic subset is semi-algebraic has as graph the closure of that restricted graph inside domain × target, so it is semi-algebraic too. Hence the finite atlas \bar{V_i} of §3.1 (after the chart refinement of E23) has semi-algebraic transitions. This gives S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M,K} an ℝ_alg-definable manifold-with-corners structure extending the one of Theorem 1.1(1). Defence: I could not consult [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2] (the paper is paywalled). But whatever coordinates it uses, the atlas above is the one the paper attributes to [BJ06a, Prop. 6.3], so the remark's conclusion fails. The remark is not used anywhere, so affects nothing is right. It is a false assertion, not a slip, so kind error is right.

review.reason: Quotation confirmed on p. 928 (author p. 13 identical). (i) The reduction needs the chart biholomorphisms S̄_i ≅ Δ^n to be definable for the R_an-structure of S̄. An arbitrary biholomorphism onto a polydisk need not be definable: in dimension one, a Riemann map of a simply connected domain with non-definable boundary is an example. The standard remedy, charts that are restrictions of charts on neighbourhoods of the closures, is not stated, and E1 forces such buffered charts anyway. (ii) 'Without loss of generality r_i = n and l_i = 0' replaces (Δ*)^r × Δ^l by (Δ*)^n, which drops the locus where one of the last l coordinates vanishes. Definability there needs a closure or continuity argument, or the observation that the proof of §4.2 works verbatim with the coordinates t_j ∈ Δ used directly for the trivial-monodromy factors. Both steps are routine and change no statement.

review.reason: Confirmed on p. 931. Two of the first reading's three points stand. (a) The map v ↦ e^v F on ⊕_(p<0) g^(p,q) is an open embedding onto the open cell of Ď opposite to the stabilizer of F, not onto all of Ď. So 'a unique holomorphic lift v(t)' with g: Δ^n → G(C) exists only while Ψ(t) stays in that cell, i.e. near t = 0 unless the polydisk is shrunk. (c) Kashiwara's Theorem 3.4.1 (p. 870, checked) gives the estimates only where y_ν > M, and Theorem 3.4.2 only on a neighbourhood of x_0, whereas Theorem 4.8 asserts them on all of Σ_n (y_n > 1). They do hold there, but only after rescaling q or a compactness argument over the closed e^(−2π)-polydisk (at a boundary point where some t_j ≠ 0, the ordering forces y_(j+1), …, y_n to be bounded too, and Kashiwara applies with fewer filtrations). The paper never says so. Point (b) is not a separate issue. p(Σ_n) lies in the closed e^(−2π)-polydisk, which is compact inside Δ^n, and the paper uses 'restricted' to mean 'the restriction to a relatively compact set of a real analytic map' (p. 929). So once v and g exist on Δ^n, their entries on p(Σ_n) are in O without analyticity near the closed unit polydisk. The shrinking is signalled by '(after maybe shrinking the polydisk)' in Lemma 4.2, and Theorems 4.1 (as corrected in E1) and 1.3 are local, so this is a routine gap with no effect on any statement in this range. Theorem 1.5 for all η (§4.5) is outside this range.

review.reason: Quotation confirmed on p. 929 (author p. 13 identical): '{(x, y) ∈ H | 0 < x < 1, 1 < y}'. The observation is correct. e(x+iy) = e^(−2πy)e^(2πix) with 0 < x < 1 misses arg q = 0, so p(𝔖_H^n) omits the points where some q_j is positive real, and the reduction to 𝔖_H^n does not literally cover a punctured polydisk. But the paper calls this set 'the usual Siegel fundamental set', and a fundamental set for z ↦ z+1 must meet the line x = 0 mod 1. So the strict inequality is a slip whose meaning is clear. With 0 ≤ x < 1, Lemma 4.2, its proof and the appeal to Theorem 1.5 (whose region |Re z| ≤ R is closed) go through verbatim. I would record it as a misprint, not a gap. The same open strip reappears in Σ_n (Definition 4.4) and in the covering claim of §4.5, which is outside this range.

sourceIssues.printed: We say that f ∈ O(x, y) is roughly polynomial if it is of the form g/h where g ∈ O[x, y, y^{−1}] and h is roughly monomial. Note that roughly polynomial functions form a ring which we denote T_n.
sourceIssues.correction: Require the denominator h to be a roughly monomial element of O[x,y,y^(−1)] (complex coefficients allowed for complex-valued functions). Then g/h + g'/h' = (gh' + g'h)/(hh') stays in the class, so T_n is a ring. In the proof of Lemma 4.7(3), write (4.4) over the denominator B(γ w_det K^(i−1))·B(γ w_det K^i), which lies in O_C[y] and is roughly monomial up to a constant phase by part (2), instead of dividing by the ratio (4.2).
sourceIssues.reason: As printed, h may be any roughly monomial element of O(x,y), and the sum of two roughly polynomial functions need not be roughly polynomial. Counterexample on Σ_1: let c = (x−1/2)² + y^(−2) ∈ O[x,y,y^(−1)] and k = (c + y^(−1))/(c + 2y^(−1)) ∈ (1/2, 1), so k ∼ 1. Then 1/k (g = 1, h = k) and −1 are roughly polynomial, but 1/k − 1 = y^(−1)/(c + y^(−1)) is not. Suppose it equals g/h with h ∼ y^s. Then g = h/(yc + 1). Write g = P(x,y) + O(y^A e^(−2πy)) with P ∈ R[x,y,y^(−1)], since the coefficients in O are analytic in q with |q| = e^(−2πy). For fixed x ≠ 1/2, |g| ≪ y^(s−1), so every y^j-coefficient of P with j ≥ s vanishes at every x ≠ 1/2, hence identically. But at x = 1/2, g ≫ y^s, a contradiction. The ring property is used in 'Proposition 4.6 follows immediately from Lemma 4.7' (sums over I-components) and in h(u,v) = Σ_i h(ũ_i,ṽ_i). Both hold with the repaired definition. The author copy is identical, and the erratum is silent.

review.reason: Quotation confirmed (pp. 929–930; author p. 14 identical). As defined, h may be any element of O(x,y) that is ∼ a monomial on Σ_n. Products stay in the class, but sums need not. I rederived the counterexample on Σ_1 = {0 < x < 1, y > 1}. Take c = (x−1/2)² + y^(−2) and k = (c + y^(−1))/(c + 2y^(−1)) ∈ O(x,y). Since c > 0, 1/2 < k < 1, so k ∼ y^0 and 1/k = 1/k is roughly polynomial; −1 is too. Their sum is 1/k − 1 = y^(−1)/(c + y^(−1)). Suppose it equals g/h with g ∈ O[x,y,y^(−1)] and h ∼ y^s. Then g = h/(yc+1). Each coefficient a ∈ O is analytic at q = 0 with |q| = e^(−2πy), so g = P + O(y^A e^(−2πy)) uniformly, with P ∈ R[x,y,y^(−1)]. For fixed x ≠ 1/2, yc + 1 ≥ y(x−1/2)², so |P(x,y)| ≪_x y^(s−1). Hence every y^j-coefficient of P with j ≥ s vanishes on (0,1)∖{1/2}; these coefficients are polynomials in x, so they vanish identically, and P(1/2,y) = O(y^(s−1)). But at x = 1/2, yc + 1 = 1 + 1/y ≤ 2, so g ≥ y^s/(2C): a contradiction. (Numerically, 1/k − 1 → 1 at x = 1/2 and ≈ 1/(0.04y) at x = 0.3.) So the stated claim 'roughly polynomial functions form a ring' is false. The ring property is used when Proposition 4.6 is said to follow 'immediately' from Lemma 4.7 (sum over I-components; §4.5 applies Proposition 4.6 to rational basis vectors e_i, not I-vectors). It is used again when h(u,v) = Σ_i h(ũ_i,ṽ_i) is summed after each term is shown roughly polynomial with the non-polynomial denominator (4.2). The repair covers both uses. B(γa,γb) = Q(g(q)a, e^(−2iy·N) ḡ(q) b̄) lies in O_C[y], and B(γ w_det K^i) has constant phase ±1 or ±i on the connected Σ_n. So (4.4) can be written with the denominator B(γ w_det K^(i−1))·B(γ w_det K^i), which is polynomial and, up to that phase, roughly monomial by Lemma 4.7(2). No numbered result becomes false: Lemma 4.5, Proposition 4.6, Lemma 4.7 and Theorem 1.5 hold with the narrower class. The false stated claim is the unnumbered ring assertion; T_n is not used again. The erratum is silent.

review.reason: Confirmed on p. 931. Theorem 4.8 is stated for u ∈ J^σ_C, a piece of a rational splitting. Lemma 4.7(1) and (2) concern u ∈ I^α, a piece of the complex splitting adapted to F as well. The needed statement is in the cited source. I checked Kashiwara pp. 860–861 and 870: Theorem 3.4.1 is stated in the sense of Definition 1.9.3, i.e. condition (1.9.5) for a splitting, and Corollary 1.9.2 shows that condition is independent of the adapted splitting. Theorem 3.4.2 allows any adapted splitting U_p. So the gap is closed by the source, but the proof as written rests on a restatement too narrow for its use. The same applies to part (2), where Lemma 4.10 is combined with Theorem 4.8(2) for wedge powers of I-vectors.

review.reason: The display on p. 932 matches the quotation. Recomputation: γ = e^{z·N}g(p(z)) with g = e^{v}. Then γ^{−1}∂_{z_i}γ = g^{−1}N_i g + e^{−v}∂_{z_i}e^{v} = e^{−ad v}N_i + ((1−e^{−ad v})/ad v)(∂_{z_i}v). Horizontality of γF means that this lies in F^{−1}𝔤 (F = Ψ(0)). For n = 1 the rest of Σ_1 is relatively compact, so the comparison holds there by continuity. For n ≥ 2, Σ_n ∩ {1 < y_n < Y_0} is not relatively compact (y_1 → ∞), and there the t_n g_n-term is of the same order as h(e^{zN}u). review.reason: The quotation matches the p. 932 image. The proof writes γu − e^{zN}u = Σ_i t_i e^{zN}g_i(t)u and bounds the ratio |t_i|² h(e^{zN}g_i u)/h(e^{zN}u) by |t_i|² times a monomial in y_i,…,y_n. On Σ_n that monomial is at most y_i^A, and e^{−4πy_i}y_i^A is bounded for y_i>1. By the triangle inequality, the upper bound h(γu) ≪ h(e^{zN}u) therefore holds on all of Σ_n. The lower bound needs the perturbation to be small, which the proof obtains only for y_n ≥ Y_0(ε). For n = 1 the remainder {0<x<1, 1<y≤Y_0} has compact closure in 𝔥, so continuity and positivity (u ≠ 0) finish the argument. For n ≥ 2, Σ_n ∩ {y_n ≤ Y_0} contains points with y_1 → ∞. There |t_n| ≥ e^{−2πY_0}, and the t_n-term is of the same order as h(e^{zN}u). The printed 'whence the claim' gives no lower bound there. The lemma is very likely true on all of Σ_n: one route is parametric norm estimates, another is uniform bounds on A_z = γe^{−zN} and its inverse via asymptotic orthogonality. Neither argument is in the paper. Defence: the paper says the lemma is 'also proven in [CKS86, Theorem 5.21]'. As later authors quote it (e.g. arXiv:2302.10200, Thm 2.1), that theorem holds on regions {log|s_1|/log|s_2| > ε, …, −log|s_n| > ε}, which include bounded y_n. I did not check that it covers h(γu), which is not the norm of a flat section. §4 also allows shrinking the polydisk (Lemma 4.2), and shrinking repairs everything needed for Theorem 1.3. This gap is the local cause of part of E56; cross-reference the two.

review.reason: Confirmed on the pp. 931–932 images. Theorem 4.8 is stated for u ∈ J^{s_1,…,s_n}_ℂ, where J is the rational splitting. Lemma 4.7 is for u ∈ I^α, and its part (2) is finished with Lemma 4.10 and Theorem 4.8(2). The decisive use is u = w_{det K^i} ∈ Λ^iV, an I-vector: the lower bound on B(γw_{det K^i}) supplies the denominators in (4.4). The I-splitting also splits F (F^s = ⊕_{p≥s}I). Example: n = 1, a Hodge–Tate limit that is not ℝ-split; there I^{1,1} = F^1 is not a rational line. Such a u equals u_σ plus lower J-components. The upper bound follows by the triangle inequality because f_{σ′} ≤ f_σ on Σ_n. The lower bound does not follow, because the components are not h-orthogonal and f_{σ′}/f_σ need not tend to 0 on Σ_n. Here u ∈ I^α has nonzero image in the multigraded quotient, and g_i(t)u needs only the upper bound. The root is Theorem 4.8 on p. 931, so also list that locator.

review.reason: The quotation matches the p. 932 image. Write a = γw_{det K^{i−1}} and b = γw_{det K^i} = a∧γw_i. Taking Schur complements of the Gram determinant gives B(u,w̃_i) = B(a∧u,b)/B(a), which is (4.3), and B(w̃_i,v) = B(b,a∧v)/B(a). The literal numerator of (4.4) is therefore P/B(a)², with P = B(a∧u,b)B(b,a∧v) ∈ 𝒪[x,y]. It is in general not in 𝒪[x,y,y^{−1}]. Example: n = 1, a nilpotent orbit whose Hodge–Tate limit is not ℝ-split, w_1 = e_1 + c e_{−1} with Im c ≠ 0. Then B(γw_1) = c_0 + c_1y with c_0 ≠ 0, and 1/(c_0 + c_1y) has an infinite expansion in powers of 1/y. It therefore lies in no 𝒪[x,y,y^{−1}]. Combining with (4.2) gives h(ũ_i,ṽ_i) = i^{2p_i−k}P/(B(a)B(b)): a polynomial over a product of roughly monomial functions, hence roughly polynomial. So the intended meaning is clear and the conclusion holds. The same text appears in the author copy and arXiv v2.

review.reason: Theorem 1.5 (p. 921, image) asserts the inclusion for 𝔥^n_{R,η} = {|Re z_j| ≤ R, Im z_j ≥ η} for all R, η > 0 (the printed C in place of R is E11). (i) R: even for small R the symmetric strip [−R,R] leaves (0,1). The fix uses Φ̃(z+k) = T^kΦ̃(z) with T^k ∈ Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) and Remark 2.6(1), which I verified: G(ℚ)-translates of Siegel sets are Siegel sets. (ii) η < 1: the region where some y_j ∈ [η,1] while others tend to ∞ is not compact. It needs a compactness argument over the closed polydisk {|t_j| ≤ e^{−2πη}}, using local charts at points of the boundary strata with trivial-monodromy factors. That region stays inside the open polydisk, so the outer-boundary problem of E1 does not arise and the theorem is very likely true. Through Lemma 4.10 (E53), the proof in fact covers only the part of 𝔖^n_𝔥 with y_n large. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.2 (p. 929) uses Theorem 1.5 only for 𝔖^n_𝔥 and the charts of §4.1 can be shrunk. Related to E1, E2 and E53 but not a duplicate of any of them. The estimates on Σ_n are uniform inequalities between continuous functions, so they extend to the closure 0 ≤ x_j ≤ 1 with the constants enlarged.

sourceIssues.printed: Notice that any connected Hodge variety is in particular an arithmetic quotient and that any Hodge morphism of connected Hodge varieties is in particular a morphism of arithmetic quotients.

For neat Γ' this image lies in G''(Q): the quotient ρ̄(P')/G'' is an R-anisotropic Q-torus, whose arithmetic subgroups are finite, and a finite neat group is trivial. Pass if necessary to a finite-index subgroup (a finite cover of the source), which does not change Y. Alternatively, use erratum Cor. 1.3 directly for morphisms of pure Hodge manifolds.

review.reason: I checked the quote on the image of p. 933. The author copy is the same. By §1.1, a morphism of arithmetic quotients comes from a morphism φ of semisimple Q-groups. The connected Hodge varieties of [K17, §3.3] are Γ\D^+ for a reductive P, and Hodge morphisms come from ρ : P' → P, which need not map Z(P') into Z(P). With the adjoint presentation that §1.3 uses, the claim is false in simple cases. Take the Hodge morphism from a product of modular curves to A_2, with P' = GL2 ×_{G_m} GL2 ⊂ GSp4. Any φ : PGL2 × PGL2 → PGSp4 inducing it would have to agree with SL2 × SL2 → PSp4, since the difference is a continuous map into the finite pointwise stabiliser of the image of H×H. But the latter does not kill (1,−1). The claim becomes true only after re-presenting the source through the image of the derived group, which here is (SL2×SL2)/±1, not the adjoint group. It may also need a finite-index subgroup, i.e. a finite cover of the source. So the 'in particular' needs an argument. The images Y, and hence the definability of special subvarieties, are unchanged. Erratum Cor. 1.3 treats morphisms of Hodge manifolds directly, which makes this remark unnecessary for §5.

sourceIssues.printed: The map f is a period map, hence is R_an,exp-definable by Theorem 1.3.
sourceIssues.correction: (a) Pull back along f the weight-0 polarized Z-VHS on D = G/K given by the adjoint representation on g with a Γ-stable lattice, polarized by minus the Killing form. Griffiths transversality is automatic because D is Hermitian symmetric. Use the adjoint representation rather than an arbitrary faithful one, which need not carry a VHS when G is not adjoint. Since Γ is torsion free, Γ ∩ Z(G) = 1 and S_{Γ,G,K} = S_{Γ^ad,G^ad,K^ad}. (b) Write f = ι∘Φ_S, with Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S, f^*V) the period map of Theorem 1.3 (its group is the adjoint group of MT(f^*V), possibly smaller than G). ι is a Hodge morphism, definable by erratum Cor. 1.3. Alternatively, note that the proof of Theorem 1.3 applies verbatim to the period map of f^*V into Γ\D. (c) If a finite étale cover of S is used, descend algebraicity: the graph of f is the image of the graph of the lifted map under a finite map.
sourceIssues.reason: Theorem 1.3 concerns the period map Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S,V) of a given VHS, not an arbitrary holomorphic map to S_{Γ,G,K}. The identification of f with a period map, the factorisation through a Hodge morphism and the finite-cover descent are all left implicit. Each step is standard and true. The Hodge morphism is also where Theorem 1.1 (the §4.6 heading) really enters.

review.reason: I checked the quote on the image of p. 933. The author copy is the same. Theorem 1.3 (p. 920) concerns Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S,V), after a possible finite étale cover. Its target is built from the adjoint group of the generic Mumford–Tate group of V and a suitable Γ. An arbitrary holomorphic f : S → S_{Γ,G,K} is the period map of the pulled-back VHS: transversality is automatic because D is Hermitian symmetric. But Hod^0(S, f^*V) is built from MT(f^*V), which can be strictly smaller than G, e.g. when f(S) lies in a proper special subvariety such as a Hecke translate of a modular curve in A_2. So f = ι∘Φ_S with ι a Hodge morphism. The definability of ι is not automatic. It is exactly the functoriality that erratum §1.1 says fails for general morphisms of arithmetic quotients, and that erratum Cor. 1.3 restores for Hodge morphisms. Another route is to observe that the proof in §§4.1–4.5 works for period maps into Γ\D whenever D is an orbit of a group containing the Mumford–Tate group. The paper says neither. So 'f is a period map, hence definable by Theorem 1.3' skips a real step. Borel's theorem is true and the repair is standard, hence 'the proof'. This is distinct from E14 (the heading) and E29 (smoothness of S).

Theorem 1.3 makes the graph of f definable for the R_an,exp-structure on S_{Γ,G,K} that extends the Theorem 1.1 structure (p. 920). Theorem 4.13 needs definability for the structure induced by the algebraic structure of S × S_{Γ,G,K}. On p. 919 the paper says the R_an-structures from Borel–Serre and Baily–Borel differ. It asserts without proof that the map BS → BB is R_an,exp-definable, and adds 'As we won't need this result in this paper'. Yet §4.6 needs exactly its consequence on the interior: the two R_an,exp-structures on S_{Γ,G,K} coincide. §4.6 never invokes this, so the printed proof has a missing step. §5 is unaffected: there only the source S carries its algebraic structure, and Y and Φ_S are definable for the Theorem 1.1 structure. Both proposed repairs work. With KUY16's fundamental set F covered by finitely many Siegel sets, the graph of the identity is the image of F under (π_{1.1}, π_{BB}), which is definable. Alternatively, S_{Γ,G,K} is smooth quasi-projective by [BB66], and Theorem 1.3 applied to the identity (the period map of the adjoint VHS) makes the identity definable from the algebraic structure to the Theorem 1.1 structure. The inverse of a definable bijection is definable. The second route avoids [KUY16]. This is the same gap as E59 (§1.2 p. 919 / §4.6), so the two should be recorded once. The same place also has: Both quotes are exact on the images (p. 919 and Remarks 1.4(2) on p. 921), and the author copy is the same. Proof of Theorem 4.12 (p. 933): 'f ... is R_an,exp-definable by Theorem 1.3. The graph of f is thus a ... R_an,exp-definable subset of the smooth complex algebraic manifold S × S_{Γ,G,K}.' The step fails as written. The structure on the target in Theorem 1.3 is explicitly the one 'extending the R_alg-definable manifold structure defined in Theorem 1.1' (p. 920), which is induced by Borel–Serre. Theorem 4.13 needs definability for the canonical structure of the algebraic manifold S × S_{Γ,G,K}, which is induced by Baily–Borel. On p. 919 the paper says these differ at the R_an level. It asserts, without proof ('As we won't need this result'), that the map BS → BB is R_an,exp-definable, and that is exactly the comparison §4.6 silently uses. So a needed step is missing and its only statement in the paper is unproved. The gap is easily filled, so Theorem 4.12 (Borel's theorem) stands. (a) Internally: S_{Γ,G,K} is smooth quasi-projective (§1.1, Baily–Borel). Put the tautological integral variation on it, for instance a Γ-stable lattice in g with Hodge structure Ad∘h_x. Up to a finite étale cover, its period map is the identity. So Theorem 1.3 makes id: S^alg → S^Thm1.1 R_an,exp-definable, and its inverse has the same graph. For M = K the Theorem 1.1 structure is canonical (erratum Remark 1.1(2)). (b) Alternatively, [KUY16, Theor. 1.9] together with Theorem 1.1(1), using that the KUY fundamental set is a finite union of translates of Siegel sets; the first reading's version is correct, with its proviso. Route (a) also settles the first reading's 'open point': recovering Borel's theorem then uses only Baily–Borel quasi-projectivity, which Borel's statement presupposes anyway, and not [KUY16]/[AMRT75]. Distinct from E29 (smoothness of S) and from the separate need to route f through a Hodge morphism (erratum Cor. 1.3).

sourceIssues.locator: §4.5, Claim and proof of the Claim, p. 933
sourceIssues.printed: Claim. There is a basis e = {e_i} of H_ℚ and C > 0 such that h_z is (e, C)-reduced for all z ∈ Σ_n. … it follows that h_z is (e, C_τ)-reduced for p(z) restricted to any curve τ in Σ_n.
sourceIssues.correction: Claim′: there are a basis e of V_ℚ with each e_i ∈ J^{σ_i}, and C > 0, such that for all z ∈ Σ_n, h_z satisfies conditions (1) and (3) of Definition 4.11 for e. Conditions (1) and (3) do not depend on the ordering, so h_z is (σ_z e, C′)-reduced for any C′ > max(C,1), where σ_z sorts the values h_z(e_i). Hence ι∘Φ̃(Σ_n) ⊂ ∪_{σ∈S_m} T_{σe,C′}, a union of m! reduced sets with m = dim V. The curve statement should read: along each curve τ, h_z satisfies (1) (and (3)) for e with a constant C_τ.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample showing the Claim fails for every basis. Take V = V_a ⊗ V_b over (Δ*)^2, where V_a is H^1 of a Tate-curve family in t_1 and V_b is Sym^2 H^1 of one in t_2. On Σ_2, h_z is uniformly comparable to diag(y_1^s y_2^b) in the integral basis e_{s,b}, s ∈ {±1}, b ∈ {−2,0,2}. If h_z were (f,C)-reduced on Σ_2 for one basis f, then h_z(f_i) ≍ λ_i(h_z)² by (2), (3) and Minkowski's second theorem. At (y_1,y_2) = (Y,Y) and at (Y³,Y) the third minimum is ≍ Y^{-1}. This forces f_1, f_2, f_3 into span(e_{−1,−2}, e_{−1,0}), which is impossible. The same example shows that no fixed ordering satisfies (2) along both the curve z_1 = z_2 and the curve z_2 = ζ. So the printed Claim and the curve statement are false. The following sentence ('we may assume (2) as there are only finitely many orderings') shows the intended Claim′. Claim′ is what the argument proves, and it gives Theorem 1.5, which asserts finitely many Siegel sets, consistent with GGLR's |I| = 1 counterexample. Same root as E3, but a different statement. Not in the erratum; the author copy p. 18 is identical.

review.reason: Quotations confirmed on the p. 933 image; the author copy and arXiv v2 are identical. I checked the counterexample and it holds. Take V = V_a ⊗ V_b over (Δ*)², with V_a = H^1 of the Tate family in t_1 (τ = z_1) and V_b = Sym²H^1 of the Tate family in t_2. The Hodge norm on H^1 in the integral basis is (m+nx)²/y + n²y, which is ≍ diag(y^{−1},y) uniformly for 0<x<1, y>1. Comparability passes to Sym² and to tensor products, so h_z ≍ diag(y_1^s y_2^b) in the integral basis e_{s,b}, s ∈ {±1}, b ∈ {−2,0,2}. This agrees with the monomials of Theorem 4.8 (s_1 = s, s_2 = s+b). Suppose h_z were (f,C)-reduced on Σ_2 for a ℚ-basis f. Condition (2) gives λ_i² ≪ h(f_i). Condition (3) together with Minkowski's second theorem gives Π h(f_i) ≪ det ≍ Π λ_i². Hence h(f_i) ≍ λ_i², and the successive minima for ⟨f⟩ and V_ℤ agree up to constants. At (Y,Y) and at (Y³,Y), both in Σ_2, the sorted exponents are (−3,−1,−1,1,1,3) and (−5,−3,−1,1,3,5), so λ_3² ≍ Y^{−1} at both points (checked numerically). Then f_1, f_2, f_3 have zero coefficient on every e_{s,b} with s+b ≥ 1 or 3s+b ≥ 1. That leaves only span(e_{−1,−2}, e_{−1,0}), which is 2-dimensional: a contradiction. So the Claim fails for every basis. For the J-adapted basis e, h(e_{1,−2}) ≍ Y^{−1} and h(e_{−1,2}) ≍ Y along z_1 = z_2, while the order is reversed along z_2 = ζ. No fixed ordering satisfies (2) on both curves, so the curve statement is false as printed. Conditions (1) and (3) do not depend on the ordering. The printed argument therefore proves Claim′, and sorting gives finitely many reduced sets, which suffices for Theorem 1.5. The finding has the same root as E3, which the ledger records with affects 'nothing'; the two reaches should be harmonized or the entries cross-referenced. Correction to the proposed text: the number of orderings is (dim V)!, not n!.

summaryBefore: The corrected paper supplies fixed-K semialgebraic arithmetic quotients and compatible morphisms, finite Siegel containment, definable algebraic-base period maps and algebraicity of exceptional Hodge-locus components. This partial continuation adds a quantitative finite-permutation basis-transfer proof, finite-relation properness and a buffered-chart transition proof; imports Cholesky and adjugate inverse instead of re-planning them; and checks 29 unreviewed source findings against the published copy. Original reduction, Hodge-analytic, finite-chart and algebraization prerequisites remain explicitly open.
